title: Problems with Fractions of a Unit

steps.body: Measurements often land between whole units. A line plot in quarter-inches records eight marks at 1/4, and four of them rebuild one inch.
steps.narration: Measurements often land between whole units. A line plot in quarter-inches records eight marks at 1/4, and four of them rebuild one inch.

widget.prompt: On a QUARTER-unit line, place where 8 quarter-marks reach.

commonPlacements.feedback: One quarter-mark is a single jump; eight of them were recorded.
4/4 is one whole unit; eight quarter-marks reach twice that.

widget.successFeedback: 2/4 of the way — but as a length, eight quarter-units is two whole units.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — count the quarter-jumps the marks represent.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — the target sits at the halfway mark on this line.

predict.reveal: Four quarter-inches make one inch, so eight of them group into exactly two.

cml.actionGoal: Hold the quantity fixed while the unit changes, and watch which way the NUMBER moves for g4v fraction unit.
invariants: Converting never changes how much there is: a smaller unit needs more of them and a bigger unit needs fewer, so the number moves in the opposite direction to the unit size in g4v fraction unit.
misconceptions: Multiplying when converting to a bigger unit, adding the conversion factor instead of multiplying by it, or comparing bare numbers across different units.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the unit got ten times smaller, what would happen to the number that measures the same object?

widget.prompt: A line plot records a total of 20 quarter-unit marks. What length do they represent in units?

commonErrors.feedback: 20 counts the quarter-marks; four of them rebuild one whole unit.
That multiplied by four. Quarter-units are SMALLER than units, so the number of units is fewer.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Name the quantity and the conversion factor, then decide whether the count should grow or shrink.

widget.prompt: A line plot records lengths in quarter-inches. Eight marks sit at 1/4 inch. What total length is that?

options.label: 2 inches, because four quarter-inches make one inch
options.feedback: Correct — eight quarter-inches group into two whole inches, since each inch holds four of them.

options.label: 8 inches, because there are 8 marks
options.feedback: The marks count QUARTER-inches, not inches; eight of them is far less than eight inches.

options.label: 32 inches, because 8 × 4 = 32
options.feedback: Multiplying by four goes the wrong way — quarter-inches are smaller, so the inch count is fewer.

options.label: 1/2 inch, because 8 is bigger than 4
options.feedback: Eight quarter-inches is two whole inches; comparing the bare numbers ignores the unit.
